en: The only good move: the queen hits e5 and prepares …Nd5.
Defend d4 and prepare c3: the f2 square stays solid.
Develop and prepare Nde2 or Be2, without panicking.
Black defends d4 with a piece rather than giving it back. One Black player in four, and the course only planned for …Nf6.
A cautious waiting move — nearly one Black player in five — stopping Ng5 but leaving d4 hanging. The course said nothing about it.
Nearly six Black players in ten release the tension here, and the course only saw …Nd7. They hand us the centre to avoid being squeezed.
The queen in the centre is quite safe here: no black knight can dislodge her with tempo — that is exactly what the trade removed.
We decline the queen trade. Black still has a king in the centre and two pieces to develop: keeping queens keeps the pressure.
We offer a second pawn to open the c-file and the diagonal: the spirit of the Scotch Gambit — time is worth more than material while Black's king sits in the centre.
The move to know: the check uncovers the queen against the e4 knight. Black regains the material but their king has lost castling for good.
Since they do not defend it, we simply take it back: there is no gambit any more, we play an ordinary Scotch with a free tempo.
We take, and the trap that follows must be known: recapturing at once with …Nxe4 loses the queen to Qe2. It is …d6 first, always.
The knight retreats rather than trade: the c5 pawn has weakened d5 and b5, two squares our pieces will occupy undisturbed.

The course assumes the Open Sicilian. Here White avoids it, and nothing answered this move.
The classical move: …d6 with both knights already out, no …a6 or …g6.
The Richter-Rauzer Attack: the pin on f6 leads to very concrete, opposite-castled play.
The quiet development; Black grabs the centre with the Boleslavsky …e5.
The bishop eyes f7/e6 (Sozin). With Be3+Qe2+0-0-0 it's the razor-sharp Velimirovic Attack.
The English Attack (Qd2, 0-0-0, g4). Here …Ng4 harasses the bishop at once.
Support f6 and open the way for the f8 bishop.
White connects the rooks, heading for 0-0-0, f4 and a pawn storm.
A typical Rauzer manoeuvre: the knight leaves d4 (dodging trades) to support e5/g5.
…e5 grabs space at the cost of the d5 hole — Boleslavsky's strategic bet.
The natural leap into the d5 hole — but it leaves e4 undefended, and that is where the line taught until now went wrong.
THE move: take the pawn. Trading on d5 first (…Bxd5) hands White a comfortable centre and costs over a point and a half.
Kick the e3 bishop and prepare …g5/…Bg7: sharp, hypermodern play.
Give up the g4 knight to take the d4 one: after hxg4, …Qa5 pins c3 and Black seizes the initiative.
Cut the diagonal first: against an early bishop sortie, that's the universal answer.

Dragon — main line
White develops the bishop first, hoping for an f7 attack. Without a centre, it never comes.
One game in five after 2…d6. Here …e6 would shut in our bishop: we develop and wait for d4.
The Dragon: the bishop heads for g7, the soul of the whole line.
White prepares the Yugoslav: Qd2, 0-0-0, h4-h5.
The quiet approach: short castling and positional play, no Yugoslav storm.
The Levenfish Attack: White charges, but …Bg7 here is premature.
The bishop to g5 rather than e3: White goes for the pin before castling long. One White player in six, and the course only planned for Be3, Be2 and f4.
The pawn props up e4 and takes g4 away: an essential prelude to the h4-h5 storm.
The queen connects the rooks; long castling is coming.
The bishop on c4 restrains …d5 and eyes f7: the Soltis variation is on the way.
When White castles without Bc4, …d5 is the classic antidote.
Develop and ready …Rc8: the c-file is the highway of Black's attack.
The rook lines up on White's king; …Nxc4 and …Rxc3 are in the air.
The Chinese Dragon: the rook swings to b8 to ram …b5-b4 home.
The knight jumps to e5, ready for …Nc4 and the exchange sac …Rxc3.
The race begins: h4-h5 to prise open the h-file against Black's king.
The Soltis reply: …h5 freezes the kingside before h5 can open lines.
White manoeuvres for Bh6 to swap off the dragon bishop.
Typical idea: the rook defends h5 sideways and nurses …b5.
Liberation: in one move the centre opens and the c3-knight is deflected.
White offers to trade the dark-squared bishops to defuse the diagonal.
Each side charges the enemy king: it's a matter of who lands first.
The knight heads to swap on b3, easing the pressure and eyeing …d5/…b5.
The right order: …Nc6 first. After …Bg7?! 7.e5 is very awkward.
Inaccurate: playing …Bg7 at once allows the following pawn thrust.
White jolts the centre; Black keeps things solid with …Nd7.
7.e5! The f6-knight is hit and the long diagonal turns against Black.
The reflex — centralise — makes it worse: Bb5+! follows and the black king will never castle. …Nfd7 was the lesser evil.
The punishment: check first. This is why …Bg7 waits its turn against the Levenfish.
One White player in five develops the bishop instead of playing d4: there will be no Dragon. The course only planned for 3.d4 — yet one game in five never gets there.
The Rossolimo: White trades on c6 to damage our structure before the Dragon even exists. One White player in eight, missing from the course.
The Alapin by transposition: White prepares d4 without ever allowing …cxd4 and Nxd4. One White player in ten, and the course had not planned for it.
The accelerated version: …g6 without …d6, saving a tempo and eyeing …d5 in one go.
Without the Maróczy bind, Black gets comfortable, active play.
The Maróczy bind: the c4+e4 pawns restrain …d5. Black plays patiently, aiming for …f5 or …b5.
One White player in five trades at once, and the course only planned for Nc3 and c4. They damage our structure before the g7 bishop takes the diagonal.
The bishop eyes f7; Black replies with …0-0, then …d6 and …Bd7.
The Gurgenidze system: …Bd7 prepares …Nxd4 then …Bc6 to hammer e4.
We cut the diagonal and prepare …d5. The c4 bishop will have to move again.
The break that settles it: the centre opens exactly when we're the better developed side.
And there's the Dragon, with a spare tempo for us: White's bishop sits on c4 rather than e2, which invites …Rc8 and …Na5.
We hit e4 at once. Without White's big centre, the Dragon fianchetto has no purpose: we play the position, not the name of the opening.
We give up the fianchetto: with a pawn on e6 the exchange on c6 loses its point, and our g8 knight goes to e7 without getting in the way.
We recapture with the b-pawn: the b-file opens for our rook and the c6 pawn will support …d5. What looks like a weakness is our plan.
We evict the bishop at once: while it sits on g5 our f6 knight — the defender of our castled king — stays pinned and White's attack arrives a tempo earlier.

5.Nc3 b5 — Hedgehog
The bishop develops first, eyeing f7. With no centre behind it, the attack never comes.
One game in seven after 2…e6. Same treatment: develop, play …b5, and the bishop loses time.
The Kan move: …a6 straight away, delaying the rest to stay chameleon-like.
The most natural development; Black usually answers …Nf6 and …Qc7.
The bind: c4+e4 stop …d5 and …b5. Black plays …Nf6, …Bb4 and works toward …d5 later.
The Hedgehog: pawns on a6-b5-d6-e6, pieces coiled, ready to spring with …d5 or …b4.
We cut the diagonal and prepare …d5. The c4 bishop must move again — two tempi lost for White.
The bishop retreats and our queenside expansion is free: precisely the kind of play a Sicilian wants.

The Najdorf assumes 2.Nf3 and 3.d4. Here White sidesteps it immediately, and nothing answered this move.
One game in five after 2…d6. Here …e6 would shut in our bishop: we develop first and wait for d4.
The Najdorf move: quiet but crucial, it controls b5 and prepares …e5/…e6.
The English Attack: White aims for Qd2, 0-0-0 and a kingside pawn storm.
The historical main line: pin on f6, extremely sharp play.
The quiet setup: White castles short and plays positionally around d5.
The Fischer-Sozin: the bishop targets e6/f7 and points at Black's king.
The positional plan: Bg2 bearing on the long diagonal and control of d5.
Adams' idea: prepare g4 without allowing …Ng4, then attack.
Kick the knight and claim the centre; in return d5 becomes a hole.
Scheveningen setup: a solid small centre, giving up …e5 to keep d5 covered.
The knight drops to b3, eyeing a5 and keeping touch with c5/d4.
The bishop watches d5, the key square of the whole Najdorf.
Supporting e4 and preparing g4 and the pawn assault.
The queen connects the rooks and prepares queenside castling.
The b8-knight heads to d7 (then b6/f8): Black's plan is …b5-b4 on the queenside.
Pawn races: both sides storm the other's king. The faster attack wins.
The pawn chases the f6-knight, guardian of d5 and e4.
Zwischenzug: instead of moving the attacked knight, hit c3 first.
Black's pawns roll on; the position is double-edged and a race move for move.
Same plan: Qd2, 0-0-0, g4. Here Black hits back in the centre with …d5.
The c3-knight retreats so it isn't kicked; d4 stays covered.
The thematic break: opening the centre while White's king is stuck on the queenside.
Support f6 and keep the structure flexible.
The e4+f4 pawn centre prepares e5 and a direct attack.
The Poisoned Pawn, Fischer's favourite: the queen grabs b2 in the opening. Ice-cold nerves required.
The queen goes to f3, then g3/h3; White castles long.
The pawn storm begins, backed by the pin on f6.
Trade off f6's defender before pushing g5, clearing the way.
The centre bursts open for the assault; razor-sharp play.
White offers b2: after the capture Black's queen is far away and exposed.
Accepting the challenge. The pawn is worth time and an attack for White.
White strikes e6 to open lines toward Black's king.
The thematic push: e5 kicks the f6-knight and rips the centre open.
The bishop covers c5 and supports a later f3/Qd2 or Nd5.
Slow manoeuvring; White presses d5, Black plays …Nbd7-b6 and …a5.
Shutting the a2-g8 diagonal and preparing …b5.
The bishop tucks into b3 before …b5 can chase it.
The queen swings to the kingside; threatening Bh6 and pressure on g7.
The break at the moment it hits the bishop: …a6 then …d5 is the standard plan against all these early sorties.
And the Najdorf arrives after all, a move order apart — with White's bishop on c4 rather than e2, which invites …Na5 and …b5.

6.f4 — opposite castling
Without 3.d4 there will be no Scheveningen. The bishop eyes f7, but with no centre the attack stays an intention.
The small centre: …e6 and …d6, flexible and solid, with …d5/…e5 in reserve.
The classical development: short castling and manoeuvring play.
The Keres Attack: g4-g5 chases the f6-knight, guardian of d5/e4. Very sharp.
The e4+f4 centre eyes e5 and f5; with Qf3 and 0-0-0 it becomes a race on the wings.
The queen comes out BEFORE …b5: the immediate push drops the a8 rook to Bxf6 gxf6 and e5.
The central break, and here it comes for free: the c4 bishop is attacked at the very moment we open the position.

With no d4 there will be no Sveshnikov. The bishop eyes f7 but, with no centre behind it, the attack never comes.
One game in five after 2…Nc6. Same treatment: …e6 first, and the bishop will lose time.
The Kalashnikov: …e5 BEFORE …Nf6, keeping the king's knight more flexible.
The Sveshnikov move: kick the knight and claim the centre despite the d5 hole.
The knight leaps to b5 to eye d6; Black will chase it and play …f5.
The pin on f6 presses d5, the key square. The whole fight is about d5.
Planting the knight on d5 at once. Black takes it and plays against the d5 pawn.
White plants a knight on d5; in return Black has the bishop pair and …f5.
The bind: c4+e4 restrain …d5. Black manoeuvres (…Be7, …Nf6, …Be6) and aims for …b5/…f5.
White pushes for space; after …d5 the e5 pawn becomes a long-term weakness.
The bishop is already relocating. We answer …Qc7 to over-defend c6 and develop without concessions.

The Nb5 jump forces …d6 (else Nd6+), then c4 sets the Maróczy bind.
The queen on c7: it presses e5 and the c-file and keeps every developing option open.
The flexible move: …a6 rules out Nb5/Bb5 and prepares …Qc7, …Nf6, …b5.
The English Attack: Qd2, 0-0-0, then f3 and g4 against Black's king.

If Black doesn't play …c6
The Slav: Black supports d5 while keeping …Bf5/…Bg4 available.
The Queen's Gambit Declined — a quarter of games. The key difference from the Slav: the c8 bishop is now shut in, and Black's whole plan follows from that.
The Queen's Gambit Accepted. Black won't keep the pawn; the point is to take it back without losing time.
Black develops before choosing a defence — one player in seven — and the course only planned for …c6, …e6 and …dxc4. We need a reply that does not let them transpose wherever they like.
The exchange: a symmetrical, safe structure, ideal for simple play with a nagging edge.
The Semi-Slav: more combative, preparing …dxc4 and …b5 with counterplay.
The key move: stopping …b5, which would hold the c4 pawn.
Preparing e4 and the Ne5 outpost. The Slav is solid but a touch passive.
One Black player in five develops this knight first, and the course only planned for …Nf6. The Exchange Slav has a drawish reputation: it only deserves it when White plays without a plan.
The Anti-Meran: pin f6 at once. The Botvinnik line is one of the sharpest in all of chess.
The Meran: White pushes e4-e5 to open the centre while Black expands on the queenside.
The most played move in this entire course — nearly six Black players in ten — and it was absent: only …c5 was planned. Black breaks the pin by developing.
The ambitious version: take the whole centre rather than regaining the pawn at once.
Black opens the way for their f8 bishop rather than contesting the centre. One player in four, and the course only saw …e5.
